newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian force commander leaves on east Zaire visit.
newsitem.headline: Canadian force commander leaves on east Zaire visit.

text.p: The Canadian commander of a proposed multinational force for Zaire left Rwanda's capital on Thursday, hoping to visit the rebel-held Zairean city of Goma, a Canadian military spokesman said.
Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril left Kigali by road in a convoy escorted by Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) troops heading for the western Rwandan town of Gisenyi, which borders on Goma.
"We don't even know whether the general is going to get into Goma. But he has left in that direction," said the spokesman.
An aide to rebel Zairean leader Laurent Kabila said earlier in Goma that Baril would meet Kabila there. Baril on Wednesday night declined to say where he would be going outside Kigali.
If he is successful, it would be his first visit to rebel-held territory since being appointed in mid-November to head the multinational force to bring aid to refugees trapped in Zaire.
The Rwandan-backed rebels, who have seized control of a swath of eastern Zaire bordering on Rwanda, have rejected any multinational force for Zaire and said they would even fire on its members.
The Zairean government says aid for refugees scattered by weeks of fighting should be sent to Rwanda to coax them home and it will only allow supplies into its territory for displaced Zaireans.
Baril said Rwandan military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame, who is vice president and defence minister, told him he saw little reason for the multinational force.
"He sees little use for force on the ground because the situation is, according to him, fixing itself quite well even though he agrees there is a lot we don't know," he said.

Kagame led his Tutsi rebels to power in Rwanda in 1994, driving the former Hutu-dominated government and its army into Zaire after their mass slaughter of up to one million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Over one million Hutu refugees fled to Zaire fearing reprisals by the Tutsi rebels, but this month an estimated 600,000 poured back into Rwanda after an alliance of Zairean rebels, including Tutsis, broke the grip of Hutu extremists on the camps.
The Rwandan government says any multinational force for Zaire is irrelevant as most Rwandan refugees have come home. Officials say it cannot use Rwandan territory for its operations.
But the U.N. refugee agency says hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced remain in eastern Zaire and need help.
"What we are trying to define precisely is what is the situation on the ground. How many folks and what condition they are in is what we are trying to find out," Baril said in Kigali.

Asked what was happening in Zaire, he said: "That's what we are trying to find out and we're putting every means that we have -- very sophisticated right down to little old me, who is going to take a look at it tomorrow."

He declined to say where he would go but added he would return later on Thursday from Kigali to Entebbe, Uganda, to compare his information with "sensors", such as aerial surveillance from U.S. and British aircraft based there.

Baril said he had not spoken to the rebels but added: "I won't hestitate because the aim is to go and take care of the folks in the field...I will go and talk to whoever I have to and that is what I am going to do."

Rebel leader Kabila argues there are few Rwandan and Burundian refugees in rebel-held territory as most have gone home to Rwanda. He says an international military presence would only serve to prop up Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The Rwandan government says aid should be sent to Rwanda for returnees, and like the rebels, says U.N. agencies exaggerated the number of refugees in eastern Zaire since 1994.
They include an estimated 100,000 former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen and their families. They headed deep into Zaire as many are wanted in Rwanda for leading the 1994 genocide.
